one_liner: SIMD Rust UTF-8/16/32 transcoder beating simdutf on most inputs, plus allocation-free grapheme/width/wrap terminal-text primitives.
what_it_does: Transcodes UTF-8/16/32 in any endianness, compares strings across encodings without converting, detects BOMs, and provides allocation-free terminal-text primitives (UAX #29 grapheme clusters, UAX #11 visible width, width-bounded truncation, greedy word wrap, in-place ANSI stripping) plus NFC/NFD/NFKC/NFKD normalization and General_Category/Script lookups. It's a #![no_std] Rust crate with its own trait-based API (Text, Encoding, Ucd), not a drop-in for simdutf's C++/validating API; the one explicit drop-in claim is for the utf8-chars crate's BufRead-to-char streaming interface.
how_it_is_fast: Ported from the C++ xstd branchless UTF kernel: UTF-8 is treated as a bit permutation, so one mask table drives both directions, with BMI2 pext gathering payload bits on decode and pdep scattering them on encode instead of per-codepoint branches or shuffle tables. Bulk paths use Rust's core::simd portable SIMD plus hand-written AVX-512 (src/x86.rs) and NEON (src/neon.rs) kernels. Decoding is also non-validating (never fails), removing the branchy error-checking state machine strict validators like simdutf must run.
when_to_use: Rust services doing bulk UTF-8/16/32 transcoding (log/network pipelines, file loaders) where simdutf's validating converters are the bottleneck, especially on emoji-heavy or mixed CJK+emoji text (+294% to +854% on UTF-16/32->UTF-8 emoji rows).

Terminal/TUI code needing fast grapheme-cluster iteration, visible-width math, or width-bounded truncation/wrap without per-call allocation (3-13x over unicode-segmentation/textwrap on the README's corpora).
Code that must decode untrusted or arbitrary bytes and can never error, rather than validating first and rejecting malformed input.
Cross-encoding equality/ordering checks (e.g. UTF-8 buffer vs UTF-16 buffer) without an intermediate String conversion.
Projects already on nightly Rust that can pin RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" builds and accept a crates.io/git dependency to that toolchain.
when_not_to_use: Need strict validation with structured decode errors (reject malformed input) — xutf is permissive/lossy by design, different semantics from simdutf's validating convert_* API.
Need a C/C++-callable library directly — it's #![no_std] Rust with zero runtime deps, not usable from C++ without writing an FFI shim.
Can't run nightly Rust: requires the core::simd/portable_simd feature, and rust-toolchain.toml only pins channel = "nightly" (no exact version).
Risk-averse production use: 10 GitHub stars, no visible issue/bug history yet to judge maturity against, and the 'Xeon x86-64' benchmark host isn't identified by exact CPU model.
Only need plain ASCII-range validation — the ASCII-only wins over simdutf are modest here (some rows within 20%, one row -1.1%), so a simpler validator may suffice.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime; #![no_std] + alloc, zero runtime dependencies (dev-dependencies only for its own benches/tests)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust nightly (portable_simd feature), edition 2024; exact nightly version not pinned
integration.platforms: x86-64 (BMI2/AVX-512 kernels when available) and aarch64 (NEON kernels); other targets fall back to the portable core::simd path, not covered by the published benchmarks
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the public API is pure functions/methods over slices and owned buffers with no global or interior-mutable state visible in src/lib.rs
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: not drop-in for simdutf (different trait-based Rust API, no_std, non-validating decode vs simdutf's validating C++ API); the README's only explicit drop-in claim is for the utf8-chars crate's streaming BufRead-to-char interface

gotchas: Decoding never fails: truncated UTF-8 sequences, lone surrogates, and garbage bytes all decode to defined-but-lossy output (e.g. a truncated sequence decodes to codepoint 0) instead of erroring — do not use where strict validation is required.
RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" is required to reach the README's peak throughput numbers; a plain nightly build without it will be slower.
UTF-16 low-surrogate encoding was deliberately changed from the original C++ xstd formula (which corrupted pairs when bit 13 of cp - 0x10000 is set, e.g. U+12000).
simdutf's non-validating convert_valid_* entry points are excluded from the README's comparison tables; only simdutf's validating convert_* path is benchmarked against.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick xutf over simdutf when you're already in pure Rust, don't need simdutf's strict validation errors, and want faster UTF-16/32<->UTF-8 transcoding plus bundled grapheme/width/wrap terminal-text helpers in one crate. Pick encoding_rs instead if you need a far more battle-tested, widely-deployed transcoder or broader legacy-encoding support beyond UTF-8/16/32 (xutf's own tables show it beating encoding_rs by roughly 1.6-8x on non-ASCII).
verified_claims_summary: Measured with a custom best-of-7 harness (not criterion; optional divan mode) on ~1 MiB ASCII/CJK/emoji corpora against the Rust `simdutf` 0.7.0 crate's validating convert_* entry points (simdutf itself calls C++ via FFI); built with nightly rustc, release profile lto="thin", RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native", on an Apple M4 Max and a second host labeled only 'Xeon x86-64'. Non-emoji transcoding margins over simdutf range -1.1% to +57.9% (below the headline 1.5-2x), while UTF-16/32->UTF-8 on emoji input reaches +294% (M4 Max) and +854% (Xeon).
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-03, v1.5.0 published on crates.io with about 32.5k downloads across 7 releases) but still a young project at 10 GitHub stars; rated 'copyable', though the nightly-only core::simd requirement and no_std/alloc design mean it can't simply be vendored into a non-Rust codebase the way a header-only C library could.
